clue.text: Too fond of pub profits?

parts.note: being 'into' something is informal for being keen on it
the bar stands for the drinking place itself
profit is gain

explanation.surface: A landlord accused of caring too much about the pub's takings.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the single word 'Too', in its sense of 'as well, besides'.
explanation.definitionFit: Too in the sense 'additionally, on top of that' is matched by this idiom meaning moreover.

clue.text: Door, open — so ___? Profit!

definitions.meaning: fills the blank: the door's open, so in troop the visitors
profit is earnings, money coming in

explanation.walkthrough: The answer read as two words completes the first phrase: 'so in come the guests'.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnings received from work or investment are a gain, matching profit.

clue.text: Cut in if they're still rocking!

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: tho, short for though, is used like 'even if'
to hew is to cut, as with an axe

explanation.surface: A plea to stop interrupting if people are still dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: The rock band of 'My Generation' still tour decades on, hence 'still rocking'.
explanation.definitionFit: The veteran British rock group continue to perform, so they are still rocking.

clue.text: Woman set about man from the outset, that's just it!

indicators.note: from the outset means taking only the opening letter of the word

parts.note: he is the male pronoun
fair means just
it is a coy word for sex or sex appeal

explanation.surface: A woman goes after a man straight away, and that's it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman set' is the definition: women as a set. 'about' is a link word, meaning 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Women collectively, an old-fashioned phrase for the female half of humanity.

clue.text: Finished what one was doing?

parts.note: split as ex (former, finished) plus act (what one was doing), and 'finished' is also an old sense of the whole word, highly finished

explanation.surface: A question about having completed one's task.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer in two: a former performance. Chambers lists 'highly finished, consummate' as a sense of the whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: Precise or consummate work is highly finished, an old dictionary sense of the word.

clue.text: Spur-of-the-moment staff-outings?

parts.note: staff 'going out' on the spur of the moment is an unofficial, sudden walkout by workers, not a works jolly

explanation.surface: Impromptu trips out for the office staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outings' suggests day trips; here staff go out in the industrial sense, downing tools without union sanction.
explanation.definitionFit: Unofficial walkouts called suddenly without a ballot are exactly impromptu departures of the workforce.

clue.text: In an endless game of tricks, East's bank set up a valid point

indicators.note: in means the following pieces are placed within the shortened game
endless means the last letter of the card game is dropped

parts.note: whist is a card game played in tricks
E is the compass abbreviation for East

indicators.note: in a down answer set up means the word is turned upside down

parts.note: a tier is a bank or row of seats

explanation.surface: A card player's bank of chips arranged during an unfinished trick-taking game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims the card game, 'set up' turns the bank upside down in this down answer, and 'In' places East and that bank within the trimmed game.
explanation.definitionFit: 'That's the crux' is said of a telling argument, a sound point hitting the heart of the matter.

clue.text: What sounds like 'Now is the winter of our discontent …' maybe

definitions.meaning: a weighted cord dropped overboard to measure the depth of water, which is sounding

definitions.text: 'Now is the winter of our discontent …' maybe
definitions.meaning: the opening words of Shakespeare's Richard III, the first words spoken in the play

explanation.walkthrough: 'sounds' is not about noise: sounding is measuring the sea's depth.
explanation.definitionFit: A plumb cord used by sailors to gauge depth, and also the opening words of a play or song.

clue.text: Pouch item from the chippy?

definitions.meaning: a flap or pouch worn over the crotch in Tudor breeches
a portion of battered fish bought at a fish-and-chip shop

explanation.walkthrough: A chippy is a British fish-and-chip shop; split the answer to get a portion of fish sold there.
explanation.definitionFit: Renaissance men wore a padded flap or bag at the front of their hose.

clue.text: With one reversal, the answer is triple layered

indicators.note: one reversal means a single pair of adjacent letters swaps places

parts.note: an answer is a reply, with the definite article in front

explanation.surface: A puzzle setter claiming the answer is layered three deep.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the adjacent E and R in THEREPLY turns it round in one place.
explanation.definitionFit: Wool or tissue made of three strands or sheets is triple layered.

clue.text: Sense perception essential for catching this when flipped?

definitions.text: Sense perception essential for catching this when flipped?

indicators.note: flipped means the hidden letters are read backwards, as a pancake is turned over
the essential part of the phrase is its inner letters, so the word sits inside it

explanation.surface: Good senses are needed to catch a tossed pancake.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: 'essential' points inside 'Sense perception', 'flipped' turns those letters round, and the clue as a whole describes the thing being tossed.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin French pancake is the thing tossed in the pan and caught, needing keen senses.

clue.text: The Great Alone, not getting on with parts by leading lady

indicators.note: not getting means the two letters that follow are dropped from the word alone

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: parts means the conjunction splits the next pair of pieces, going between them

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read 'by' as in six by four
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen, is the country's leading lady
and is a synonym of with

explanation.surface: A film or novel called The Great Alone, reworked with parts written for a star actress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Great Alone' reads as a title, but 'The Great' is the definition and 'Alone' fodder; 'not getting' drops 'on', and 'parts' sends the conjunction between the multiplication sign and the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Macedonian conqueror is known by the epithet 'the Great', so the title stands for his name.

clue.text: Am I bothered lug is lashing crew?

parts.note: meh is a slang shrug of indifference, like 'Am I bothered?'
lug is informal for an ear
ties as in lashes with rope

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs as a lout ropes up the crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Am I bothered' is the catchphrase of a stroppy teenager in British TV comedy; MEH captures the same shrug.
explanation.definitionFit: The pirate's form of address to his sailors, 'my fine fellows', calls the ship's company.

clue.text: See 6
During series a couple of players express rage I could not contain?

indicators.note: during means the later pieces fall within the abbreviation
a couple of means the first two letters of the word

parts.note: to utter is to express in words

explanation.surface: A spectator in a match series voicing anger that can't be held in.
explanation.walkthrough: SER is an abbreviation for series; 'a couple of' takes PL from 'players'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone too angry to speak clearly emits incoherent, spitting noises: the speaker who could not hold their fury in.

clue.text: Exemplary policy, Part Two missing wife out

indicators.note: missing means one letter is left out of the pool of letters
out signals the remaining letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A model scheme in which Part Two has the wife cut out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' is the anagram signal; 'missing wife' removes W from POLICYPARTTWO before the letters are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exemplary serves as the very model or original pattern of its kind.

clue.text: Suffragette will mobilise e.g. these 'pious' types

indicators.note: mobilising gets things moving, so the letters are reshuffled; the remaining letters plus these from e.g. make one pool

explanation.surface: A campaigner for votes for women rallying hypocrites.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will mobilise' shuffles the campaigner's title, which holds the answer plus the letters of 'e.g.'. Tartuffe is Molière's sanctimonious hypocrite, hence the quotation marks round 'pious'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypocrites who parade false piety are named after Molière's title character.

clue.text: The sounds one's into? Swap metal with American track by 2

indicators.note: swap means the American abbreviation in the first word is exchanged for the metal

parts.note: music is the sounds
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: with completes the swap, putting the American letters where the metal was

parts.note: one's bag is slang for what one is into

explanation.surface: A musician swapping heavy metal for an American number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music bag' is what one's into musically; 'Swap ... with' exchanges its US and AG. The track is by The Who, the answer to 2 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Who released this song in 1968, so it is a track by the band at 2.

clue.text: Mountaineer treated rare auk nursing its right wing

indicators.note: nursing means holding a letter inside the rearranged letters
treated means processed, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the auk's right wing is its last letter, K

explanation.surface: A rare seabird being treated while cradling its injured wing.
explanation.walkthrough: Jon Krakauer, climber and author of 'Into Thin Air' and 'Into the Wild', the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The American writer is a climber who wrote about the 1996 Everest disaster.

clue.text: For which one flew to launch chequered Aussie career?

definitions.text: For which one flew to launch

indicators.note: a chequered pattern is mixed up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Australian who flew off to start a varied career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'launch' looks like a verb about starting a career, but in the definition it is a noun: the boat or helicopter one flies to.
explanation.definitionFit: The emergency service at sea may send a lifeboat or helicopter, which a downed pilot would hope to reach.

clue.text: Rocky, perhaps, but ready for Panamanian

definitions.meaning: the surname of Rocky, Sylvester Stallone's boxer
the ready is slang for cash, and this is Panama's currency unit

explanation.walkthrough: 'ready' is British slang for money, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Stallone's fighter shares his name with the currency of Panama, named after the Spanish explorer.

clue.text: Everyone stripped from the waist up? Exactly!

indicators.note: in a down answer up means the letters are read bottom to top

parts.note: everybody bare-chested is wearing no tops

explanation.surface: A shout confirming that everyone is topless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' looks like part of 'from the waist up' but signals the turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation agreeing with a remark means precisely right, used as an interjection.

clue.text: Drink you're glugging like some of the black stuff!

definitions.text: like some of the black stuff

indicators.note: glugging means swallowing, so the word is taken in by the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone downing a pint of stout, the black stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The black stuff' is British slang for Guinness, but here it is ink.
explanation.definitionFit: Ink is a black writing fluid, so something resembling it is dark and stained like it.

clue.text: Star Trek providing parts for this group of players?

parts.note: a super is a star or ace
a tramp is a long hike

explanation.surface: Star Trek supplying acting roles for a troupe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star Trek' reads as the TV show; split it into two pieces. The players are musicians, the British rock band.
explanation.definitionFit: The British band of the 1970s is a group of musicians, who are players.

clue.text: From the collection of Nick Clegg, say?

definitions.text: From the collection of Nick Clegg, say?

parts.words: From the collection of Nick Clegg, say?
parts.note: a bookplate's Latin marks a book from someone's library, and Clegg is a former Liberal Democrat leader

explanation.surface: A book once owned by the former deputy prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Short for 'ex libris', written in books from a personal library; Nick Clegg led the Liberal Democrats, so he is a former 'Lib'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin bookplate phrase means 'from the books of', marking a volume from someone's library.

clue.text: Doing fine sort of skunk

parts.note: what someone is at is what they are doing
OK means fine

explanation.surface: Someone being fine with some kind of skunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What are you at?' means 'what are you doing?'.
explanation.definitionFit: A South African name for the striped polecat, a skunk-like animal.

clue.text: Giving in to flu bout, occasionally nasty

indicators.note: something turned nasty is twisted, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: occasionally takes every other letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone surrenders to a bad bout of flu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giving in' reads as a phrase; only 'Giving' is the definition. 'occasionally' takes B and U from 'bout'.
explanation.definitionFit: A generous person is giving freely, plentiful in what they hand out.

clue.text: Drive back westbound Underground passenger?

indicators.note: in an across answer westbound means read right to left

parts.note: a tuber travels underground, and jokingly is someone riding the London Tube

explanation.surface: Pushing a passenger back on a westbound Tube train.
explanation.walkthrough: The Underground is London's Tube railway; a potato-type tuber also lives underground.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel an attack is to drive it back, a sense of refuting or repulsing.
